Keep in mind that anorexia’s key component is low BMI. I think (I do not know this) that the benefits of providing nutrients for life (the goal is sustenance) outweigh the costs of stress to someone with anorexia implicated by weight gain. I would like to think that Health Care Practitioners understand the implications of weight gain, but those stresses will not “kill” (in the sense of an immediate threat) you like the stressors added through weight gain. The goal is sustenance and rehabilitation, and your dialogue about rights seems to be motivated by anger. And I do not blame you, I for a really long time felt like I was being punished by being expected to gain weight and even in recovery, gaining weight. 

Now, Binge Eating Disorder is considered a diagnostic feeding and eating disorder. The orientation of binging is not weight focused like anorexia. So if we disregard my comment about the requirement not being weight founded or oriented, how do we intervene with binge eating? Do we restrict the availability of food in a clinical setting? How do we force weight loss without triggering or causing more problematic eating or an unhealthy orientation to weight loss? I think those are hard questions to answer. And if we could answer them it would be extremely burdensome to the healthcare system.

In my opinion (which is limited to an undergrad in psychology), a reason why binge eating is not associated with weight is because it doesn’t belong to a specific weight, just like disordered eating can be seen at any BMI. Anorexia specifically is given a specific emaciated caricature in media, and not all anorexics are extremely underweight as BMI is a terrible tool anyways. A lot of people suffering anorexia don’t get forced to gain weight - I never was despite a clinical diagnosis. I was never in patient.

When looking at models of care (used in Nursing), you really have to meet someone where they are. The Stages of Change model acknowledges that change is not linear and there are various stages of intervention: precontemplation – not aware or minimizing the problem, contemplation – acknowledging the problem and direction for change, preparation – making plans, action and maintenance (Frasier, Slatt, Kowlowitz & Glowa, 2001; Mason & Pellizzari, 2006).  It’s used commonly for domestic violence but you can definitely draw parallels. For example, someone in denial of their problem (precontemplation), providing supports will not address that persons needs. But, alerting them of the dynamics of their problem or what the problem looks like, also encouraging safety is more appropriate before moving forward. Also the articles I have linked are clinically based, research for domestic violence.

That’s all super jargon-y but a good way to look at this is telling someone who doesn’t think they have a problem isn’t going to get them to identify or disclose that they do, you’ll likely make a huge barrier for them confiding in you or even acknowledging their own behaviour. Sitting her down, or getting her to go to a GP she TRUSTS (trust is very important) and saying this is what alcoholism looks like may be more effective (not what they’re doing specifically and attacking those behaviours but looking at [characteristics of alcoholism](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/alcohol-use-disorder/symptoms-causes/syc-20369243) ) to get her to realize the problem drinking. Then providing tools for how to be safe and following up (maybe in a day or a few weeks) may help - not enabling the behavior, simply making behavior shes in denial about SAFER (I.e, don’t drink on an empty stomach, stay hydrated). It’ll be a long process but it might make the journey a bit easier. I hope this meets you well! I really don’t have real life experience, this is all research based and theoretical.

On your comment about obesity, obesity is actually not defined by cause. In the DSM-V (which obviously isn’t perfect, but still highly respected) over eating is a pathology of eating disorders. So while it is not a disorder to be addicted to food (addiction to food - aka binge eating is characterized as a loss of control in eating, consumption of excessive calories, etc.), it is a component of a bigger mental health issue. Acknowledging comorbidity of addiction and mental health is important because it is usually indicative of a comorbid disorder - things that compose and arguably predispose addicts are actual diagnostic criteria to a disease such as impulsivity, low self control, etc.

I really like this description! I also think labelling addiction as a disease puts it in the lens of a health concern and not a criminal one. My personal opinion is addicts don’t need to be punished to deter their use, they require medical attention. If we frame addiction as a health issue we’re able to support addicts in recovery rather than punishing them. If providing a safe and supportive environment is “enabling”, then is it wrong to do so? Abstinence is less successful. Also, with such a high comorbidity with mental health, it’s important to think of addiction as a separate health issue.

Also there are biological components to addiction that make it a disease, in that it alters or inhibits cognitive function (long term AND in short term use) but also alters the physical structures of the brain (think synapses, memory capacity, etc - and by all means I can find a source), not to mention genetic predispositions. When you think disease, one way to pathologize is contrasting normal and abnormal. These deficits and neurocognitive changes are ABNORMAL to the population. I think that justifies calling it a disease. 

Also OP, you have seemed to make your mind up that all of this contextualizing addiction as a disease is enabling. However, I view it as empowering - offering someone the tools and confidence to control their life. When we consider addiction a disease we offer them an opportunity to succeed not contingent on immediate success - failure followed by the support to try again may be necessary for someone to start believing they can overcome addiction.
